data.long_meaning: Raji is a name of Sanskrit origin which literally means 'ruler' or 'queen'. This name signifies power, authority, and leadership. Linguistically it belongs to the Hindu tradition and is also used in Hindi, Sanskrit. Parents who choose Raji usually hope their child will grow to embody queen, ruler and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.spiritual_meaning: In Hindu mythology, Raji is also associated with the goddess Durga, who is the embodiment of strength and power. This name can inspire courage and determination, and can be a source of motivation for those who seek to lead and rule.
data.etymology: Raji belongs to the Hindu linguistic tradition and is used in Hindu naming. Its recorded meaning is “Queen, ruler.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Raji total 2, giving a life-path number of 2. Number 2 is linked with Moon and with the qualities of harmony, sensitivity and partnership.

It is believed that those named Raji are born leaders and natural born-rulers. They are expected to carry themselves with grace, dignity, and a strong sense of responsibility.
data.spiritual_significance: In Hinduism, the name Raji has a deeper spiritual significance. It signifies the innate power and spiritual authority that exists within each individual. The name encourages the bearer to embrace their inner power and lead a virtuous and righteous life, just as a ruler leads her people with wisdom and compassion. The name Raji is a reminder of one's potential to rule their own mind, emotions, and actions, and to lead a life that is guided by enlightened values.

historical_references.reference: Raji was a queen of the Chalukya dynasty in the Deccan plateau of India, who ruled in the second half of the 11th century. She is best known for her victory over the northern Chalukya king, Bhima I, which allowed her to extend her domain further north.

Another Raji was a queen of the Haihaiyas, a minor ruling dynasty in the eastern part of the Deccan plateau of India, who lived in the late 16th century. She is best known for her successful resistance against the invading Mughal forces under the command of Akbar, during which she is said to have killed Akbar's general, Malik Ambar, in a battle.
